s.t: TOPIC 3.1 — Tissue Mechanics: Concepts, Bone, Articular Cartilage, Aging
s.x: TOPIC 3.1 Tissue Mechanics: Concepts, Bone, Articular Cartilage, Aging Objectives: understand stress-strain curves, viscoelastic properties, stress relaxation, and creep.

1. Types of Loading Load What it does Example Compression Pushes together Joint compression — the femur sitting on the tibia Tension Pulls apart Tendons and ligaments — a high tensile load is the ACL tear mechanism Shear Items slide across each other The patellofemoral joint — patella sliding across the femur Torsion Twisting along an axis Bending Tension on one side, compression on the other

2. Mechanical Property Definitions Term Definition Stress Force generated by resisting deformation — force ÷ area Strain Ratio of deformed length to original length Stiffness (Young's modulus) Ratio of stress to strain — the slope in the elastic region Elastic region Material returns to its original shape after the load is removed Plastic region Material stays deformed after the load is removed Yield point Where behaviour transitions from elastic to plastic Ultimate failure point Where the material breaks Energy Area under the stress-strain curve — can be stored or dissipated 🎙 Think of the yield point as the point of no return — it's the inflection point. And the ultimate failure point is the other one. Reading the curve in tissue terms: first slack is taken up and the fibres straighten. Then the elastic region — safe, reversible stretch, like an elastic band. Then the plastic region — permanent change. Then failure — the tissue breaks. ★ The reason any of this matters: this is exactly what happens when an athlete tears something. The deck uses Kevin Durant rupturing his Achilles in the NBA Finals as the picture of ultimate failure.

3. Viscoelasticity, Creep and Stress Relaxation Term Definition Viscoelastic Behaviour changes with the rate of loading — it is velocity dependent. Load it faster and it behaves differently Creep Under a constant load , the material deforms and reaches an equilibrium state. Rapid initial deformation, then slow deformation until equilibrium Stress relaxation Under a constant deformation , stress builds initially then slowly decreases to equilibrium. It distributes the stress across the tissue — protective Biphasic Contains components with different properties (fluid + solid, organic + inorganic) Anisotropic Mechanical properties differ between loading modes — behaves differently in tension than in compression 🎙 Creep over a lifetime: as someone ages, the vertebrae eventually shrink in height. That's a form of creep — which is why older people are shorter than they were when they were younger. 🎙 Stress relaxation, made physical: stand on a bed. Your foot sinks in until it stops sinking in, and you're not breaking the bed either — it's just supporting you. That's stress relaxation. ★ Dr. Awruch flags biphasic and anisotropic as nice-to-know rather than need-to-know. Creep, stress relaxation and rate-dependence are the three the handout lists as take-home. 🎙 One forward-looking point he makes: just because something hurts, it doesn't mean there is something structurally wrong. Not very relevant for this class — very relevant later.

Quick-Reference Glossary — Topic 3.1 Term Definition Compression / tension / shear / torsion / bending The five loading modes Stress Force per unit area generated resisting deformation Strain Deformed length ÷ original length Stiffness Stress ÷ strain; the slope of the elastic region Elastic region Reversible deformation — returns to original shape Plastic region Permanent deformation Yield point Transition from elastic to plastic behaviour Ultimate failure point Where the material breaks Viscoelastic Rate-of-loading dependent behaviour Creep Progressive deformation under a constant load Stress relaxation Decreasing stress under a constant deformation Biphasic Containing components of differing properties Anisotropic Properties differ depending on the direction of loading
TOPIC 3.2 Stages of Healing Objectives: discuss the phases of tissue healing, and apply the phases to cases across different tissues.

1. Types of Injury Injury What it is Strain Musculotendinous unit — a pulled muscle. The classic one Sprain Ligamentous injury, grades I–III — the grade goes up as more of the ligament is damaged Dislocation Loss of anatomical relationship of the joint Subluxation Partial dislocation — think of it as a short-term dislocation Muscle/tendon rupture or tear Partial or complete Tendinopathy Tendon injury affected by mechanical loading — tendinitis acutely, tendinosis when it has been going on longer (inflammation, or inflammation with scar tissue) 🎙 On complete tears: it's not actually what you think. Sometimes a full tear just means it went completely through — it doesn't mean it's completely torn off. Condition What it is Synovitis Inflammation of a synovial membrane — e.g. a tendon sheath that exists to reduce friction, which sometimes gets inflamed itself Hemarthrosis Bleeding into the joint (*heme* = blood, *arthrosis* = of the joint) Ganglion Tendon or joint capsule wall ballooning — the classic ganglion cyst on the back of the hand Bursitis Inflammation of a bursa. Harder to see; often a diagnosis of exclusion on orthopaedic exam Contusion Bruising from trauma Overuse / cumulative trauma Repetitive low loads resulting in inflammation and pain 🎙 Two places Dr. Awruch corrects his own slide. First, he'd retitle this from 'types of injuries' to just 'conditions' — not all of these happen via an injury. Second, on overuse he'd drop the word 'low': common sense says repetitive HIGH loads cause overuse too.

2. SINSS Letter Meaning What it buys you S — Severity How intense and impactful is this in the person's life Determines the appropriate vigour and extent of the examination and the interventions I — Irritability What aggravates it, what eases it Same — sets how much you can do N — Nature The body system in question Directs the focus of the exam, the intervention, and whether referral is needed S — Stage Acute (<6 weeks) · subacute (6–12 weeks) · chronic (>12 weeks) Identifies the stage of healing, which guides the corresponding intervention S — Stability Improving, worsening, or not changing Identification of influencing factors 🎙 On the timeframes: there are different definitions, but what he's seen most is under 6 weeks acute, 6–12 weeks subacute, over 12 weeks chronic — with some discrepancy in the literature. ★ The stability point is the one with real clinical teeth. If a patient improves from visit 2 to 3 and again from 3 to 4, they will likely keep improving. If they keep getting worse over a long course of care, that's your cue to ask why, and to consider referral. 🎙 Why stage matters so much: if you know there's a soft-tissue injury to a muscle, and you know the tissue healing timeline for muscle, you can accurately predict when it's safe to start isometric strengthening and then isotonic strengthening.

3. The Four Phases Phase What is happening What you see on exam Duration Inflammation Vascular, cellular, chemical and immune processes; cells, chemical changes, immune cells and fibroblasts rush to the area Swelling, redness, warmth (signs) and pain (symptom). Movement is painful; PROM may produce muscle guarding before end range 4–6 days Proliferation & repair Noxious and inflammatory chemicals removed; capillary growth; collagen and granulation tissue form Decreased swelling, inflammation resolving. Pain at end-range resistance with ROM, and weakness 10 days – 6 weeks , longer in tissues with poor vascularity Maturation / remodeling Connective tissue maturation, scar tissue contracture, conversion of Type III collagen , reorganisation with stress Inflammation completely resolved. Pain only at end range of available motion, past resistance. Weakness can persist 6–12 months , variable with severity and tissue 🎙 The postoperative version of the inflammatory phase: you get a patient after a rotator cuff repair, you go to do passive range of motion, and they say stop pulling, it's really painful. You might even feel some spasm — they're just uncomfortable moving into that new range. ★ Why the 6-week mark keeps appearing in protocols: in a lot of postoperative protocols strengthening doesn't start until six weeks, which is the end of the proliferation window. Some physicians add an extra week on top. 🎙 On the 6–12 month maturation window: on paper it might last 12 months, but watching a patient perform, they're likely significantly stronger by month six or eight. You might need until the end of the year for full gains.

4. PT Goals by Phase Phase Goal Do Precautions / contraindications Inflammation Maximum protection Control the effects of inflammation (pain) · prevent the adverse effects of rest · cautious progression of movement · protective and assistive devices as indicated Contraindicated: stretching and resistance exercise to inflamed tissue Proliferation Moderate protection / controlled motion Scar mobilisation · promote healing · progress ROM with caution · progress exercise intensity Increased inflammation, or pain lasting > 24 hours Maturation Minimal protection / return to function Improve scar quality · increase strength and endurance · function-specific exercise · progress to return to work or play for high demand No inflammation, or pain > 4 hours, or pain requiring medication 🎙 A distinction worth writing down: in the inflammatory phase he would replace 'stretching' with 'range of motion'. Range of motion is typically fine — stretching, meaning actively trying to gain range, is not. And the great thing about the resistance-exercise contraindication is that if you tried, the patient would tell you it hurts anyway. 🎙 On working inside a protocol, in the proliferation phase: if the protocol says you may move the shoulder to 110°, those are your parameters — but that doesn't mean you have to go to it. Tell the patient we're allowed to take you to 100°, let me know if it hurts before we get there, and let me know if you want me to stop. Individualise to the patient These are general timeframes — health and lifestyle will change them Setbacks happen. Communicate and go back to the drawing board Understand your patient's factors; education is key Not every patient comes from a physician — with direct access you are the first one, so know the timelines and communicate Usually the patient will tell you when they feel ready for the next stage 🎙 The photo of the forest is there on purpose: in PT school information comes in pieces, and when you see a case it's easy to clutch onto one item or one test instead of stepping back. As you learn more you may find you're sure of less — and that's okay. See the forest through the trees.

TOPIC 3.3 Needs Analysis Objectives: identify the impairment bucket, identify the necessary task demands, identify the treatment bucket, and apply to cases.
1. The Impairment Bucket Bucket Treatment 1. Weakness Strengthening 2. Mobility Mobilization 3. Pain Treat the pain

Bucket 1 — Weakness Two different presentations both land here: decreased strength and hypermobility . Both are treated with strengthening. HISTORY — DECREASED STRENGTH HISTORY — HYPERMOBILITY “I get really fatigued and tired” “I've been double jointed since I was a kid” “It's hard to do” · “difficulty” “Clicking and popping” — e.g. a swimmer with shoulder symptoms Time of day is NOT consistent — worse at the end of the day, or pain only at certain times “I've had dislocations in the past” Exam finding What you may see AROM Maybe decreased — they can't lift the joint because they're too weak PROM Could be increased — they're hypermobile MMT / myotome Decreased strength Functional movements Decreased quality — squat, lunge, single-leg squat. Watch a single-leg squat and see the knee wobbling Joint mobs Normal or hypermobile Findings, either/or: decreased strength, OR increased ROM = hypermobile.

Bucket 2 — Mobility History: “hard to move it” · “feels tight” · “feels stuck” · “I can't” — and crucially, the same story any time of day . 🎙 Why the time-of-day question separates the first two buckets: if something is tight, it's going to be tight consistently. Someone getting tired after being at work all day is a very different story, and that points toward decreased strength. Exam: PROM decreased · joint mobilization hypomobile . Findings: hypomobility on joint mobs, decreased ROM, and sometimes a firm end feel . The cause is either the joint being tight or soft tissue restriction — so the treatment is stretching or mobilization.

Bucket 3 — Pain History: pain and/or fear — “it hurts when…” · “I worry that…” · “I don't want to make it worse, so I don't move.” Exam: empty end feel on ROM — pain well before end range. On MMT, pain or fear limits effort. Finding: painful, and possibly afraid of the pain.

2. Necessary Task Demands STRENGTH → STRENGTHEN MOBILITY → MOBILIZE Clinical principle: if it is NOT a mobility requirement, then by default it is a strength requirement. Strength is the default bucket Simple as this: how much ROM does the task require? Everything here requires active muscle contraction : power · agility · motor control · endurance · coordination · balance You only need enough ROM to do the task. A sprinter needs no more range than sprinting requires; a marathoner needs enough for the gait they run with. That's it Sprinter → power and endurance. Soccer player → agility. Powerlifter → power. Century-ride cyclist → endurance If a patient already has enough range for their task, they default into the strength bucket and come out of the mobility bucket — range is checked off, so the remaining limitation must be strength

3. Putting It Together Impairment bucket + task demands = treatment bucket Is ROM sufficient? Compared to normal, AND for the task needed Is strength sufficient? Compared to normal, AND for the task needed The task demands can outweigh the impairment bucket 🎙 Two examples of task demand outweighing the impairment: someone with 5/5 MMT does not necessarily have enough strength to be an Olympic weightlifter. And a competitive cyclist with 5/5 strength on testing still may not be able to ride a hundred miles — that task demands endurance, not just strength.

4. The Two Cases Case Findings Reasoning Judi , 16, high school swimmer. Bilateral shoulder pain, worse during swim season. Clicking and popping. Dislocated both shoulders years ago doing different sports Joint mobility hypermobile in all shoulder planes · ROM hypermobile (she doesn't stop at 180° of flexion, she keeps going; external rotation the same) · positive Beighton score She already has more mobility than she needs. Stretching would only make it worse. She needs strengthening Christina , 26, runner, PT student. No pain at rest or during her day, but knee pain from about mile 8 while training for the Boston marathon, resolving after the run ROM normal · joint mobility normal · MMT deficits in quadriceps, hamstrings and hips (4+/5) Pain arrives with fatigue , not consistently — that's the weakness pattern. Strengthening bucket , not stretching and not pain-based treatment

s.x: TOPIC 3.4 Intervention Decision Making — Clinical Reasoning 1–3 A three-part series. The stated starting point is “ it depends ” — and the point of the series is to turn that into a repeatable decision.

s.t: 1. What Range of Motion Tells You (Part 1)
s.x: 1. What Range of Motion Tells You (Part 1) Finding What it means So… AROM normal and pain-free You can rule that joint out as the pain generator — full range, normal end feel, no pain Add overpressure (effectively PROM) to confirm. Surrounding musculature can still be involved AROM < PROM A muscle power impairment — power is impaired, which means weakness Strengthening may be a great antidote AROM limited, and PROM can't make up the difference Some form of tightness — a mobility impairment Stretching or mobilization If AROM is limited , there are three possibilities: weakness, tightness, or pain — plus a fourth factor, fear . If PROM is limited or painful , it is one of three things: a joint mobility deficit , a tissue extensibility deficit , or pain . It is not weakness — passive motion doesn't involve muscle activation, because you are producing the movement. 🎙 On fear: if someone was hurt previously, the brain remembers that experience, similar to other forms of trauma. After a car accident a person may be fearful the next time they drive on the highway. That fear alone can limit movement. ★ The telehealth argument for why ROM is so valuable: you can't put hands on the patient or perform orthopaedic tests, so you're doing a detailed subjective history and observing range of motion — and you're still getting about 95% of the information you'd normally get in clinic. 🎙 The musculoskeletal screen and the neuro screen are performed together. They're taught in isolation in a neuro class and a musculoskeletal class, but they are not performed in isolation — nerves activate and control muscles, and any pain felt is regulated by the nervous system.

2. Matching Finding to Intervention (Part 2) Finding Pairs with Weakness Strengthening Pain Pain-focused treatment Fear Psychologically informed physical therapy Joint mobility deficit Joint mobilization or manipulation Tissue extensibility deficit Stretching 🎙 Tightness has exactly two sources. Tissue extensibility deficits is a bucket term for anything soft-tissue — muscle, ligament, nerve, scar tissue. Joint mobility deficits mean the joint itself lacks mobility. The ankle worked example — why precision matters Limited dorsiflexion could be tissue extensibility (soleus, posterior tibialis, anything behind the ankle) or a joint mobility deficit (talocrural joint) If the soleus is what's limiting it, mobilising the talocrural joint doesn't address the problem If the talocrural joint is tight and the soleus and gastroc aren't, mobilising the joint is exactly right It isn't dangerous to mobilise something that isn't tight — it's just unnecessary. You're using the wrong tool 🎙 The screwdriver analogy he keeps coming back to: if you needed a Phillips head but were given a flat head, you simply would not be able to target what you needed to target. Weakness has two flavours too. Muscle-related — quadriceps testing 3+/5, so a long arc quad targets the quadriceps in that same position. Or motor control — a single-leg squat showing knee and hip adduction, valgus collapse , which is a combination of strength deficits, motor control deficits and likely hip abduction weakness. You strengthen those areas AND retrain the movement. 🎙 On pain being inhibitory: if you've ever stepped on a pebble barefoot, you probably noticed your knee buckle immediately. Pain causes rapid inhibition — it essentially short-circuits the quadriceps and the muscles needed to load the limb. That's why your leg may feel weaker the day after a knee injury even though nothing is torn. ★ Do not treat what you do not see. A hypermobile gymnast with low back pain does not need a flexibility exercise — if nothing is tight, what exactly are you stretching? Stretching cannot fix tightness that is not present.

3. The Interventions Themselves (Part 3) Intervention Forms When Joint mobilization Self-mobilization (e.g. foam roller for limited thoracic extension) · manual therapy mobilization · manipulation Joint mobility deficit Stretching Self-stretch · therapist-performed manual stretching · massage or instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization (IASTM) Tissue extensibility deficit Manual therapy Does two things: increases ROM and reduces pain Tight joint, or a painful joint where the patient is having trouble relaxing Psychologically informed care CBT · graded exposure · relaxation therapy · pain neuroscience education · activity pacing High pain, debilitating pain, fear avoidance, chronic pain Strengthening Resistance training → motor control → power → running, cutting and return-to-sport drills Weakness, and often indirectly as graded exposure MOBILIZATION MANIPULATION Low velocity — slow, controlled force applied over time High velocity, low amplitude Gently applying force to get the segment moving and potentially reduce pain Very fast, and the amplitude is quite low — possibly lower than a mobilization Larger amplitude is possible because it's slow Move something quickly and it must be a very small movement. Large, fast movements are where things become unsafe 🎙 The CrossFit worked example for stretching: he struggles to keep his arms overhead at the bottom of an overhead squat. At the bottom the latissimus dorsi is wound up on both ends — it attaches to the pelvis and to the shoulder, so it's a bi-articular muscle. Home exercise, soft tissue work, IASTM, or a foam roller. Activity pacing — breaking the boom-bust cycle The pattern: overactivity → injury and pain → a lot of rest → return full steam → overactive again → pain again → rest even longer → weaker → repeat Instead of the full activity that causes pain — running eight miles — you have them run two Rest an appropriate amount, not long enough to become weaker , then return to the same activity Gradually progress. This is how you move patients out of chronic pain 🎙 On why strengthening works when you might not expect it: knee pain often responds well to hip strengthening as well as hamstring and quadriceps strengthening. But when pain is the primary issue and pain levels are high, strengthening may not be realistic or appropriate initially. Why the strengthening order matches protocols: look up an ACL reconstruction protocol and you'll see restore range of motion → strengthen → motor control → power → running → return to sport, all while respecting tissue healing timelines.

4. The Whole Framework, One Picture Start at the body region in question . Assess AROM — full and pain-free rules the joint out. If limited or painful, gather more: assess PROM to separate weakness from tightness from pain or fear. PROM full and pain-free → strengthen. PROM limited or painful → address the limitation, or the pain, or the fear. 🎙 This can feel overwhelming, but slow down and recognise that you already know this information. All I have done is organise it into a systems-level framework that mirrors how clinicians think. ★ If it ever feels like too much, the whole series collapses to one rule: TREAT WHAT YOU SEE. Weakness → strengthening. Tightness → stretching or joint mobilization. Pain and fear → pain modulation and psychologically informed PT.

5. The Four Part-2 Cases Patient Presentation If you could do only ONE thing Lauren , 36, fell on an outstretched arm skiing. Left shoulder pain AROM: can't reach overhead fully (beyond ~125°) · PROM full · resisted ER weak and mildly painful · flexion 2+/5 · resisted IR normal Rotator cuff strengthening. PROM is full so there's no tightness; her pain is mild and she isn't fearful Olivia , 26, ballet dancer, fell on her patella. Severe knee pain X-rays negative · ROM limited to 95° flexion due to pain Address the pain. Strengthening or stretching would likely make things worse at this stage Sarah , 23, three weeks post knee arthroscopy. Fearful of bending the knee, worried about 'ruining the surgery' (a teammate needed a second surgery) ROM −10° extension to 95° flexion · no end feel , but she grimaces and asks you to stop · she says it doesn't hurt at all — she's afraid it might Psychologically informed physical therapy. The limiter is fear, not tissue Brian , 55, knee osteoarthritis with tight hamstrings and quadriceps ROM limited with a firm end feel and minimal pain Stretching and joint mobilization

s.t: TOPIC 4.1 — Therapeutic Exercise Prescription Principles — FITT-VP, What Matters Most
s.x: TOPIC 4.1 Therapeutic Exercise Prescription Principles — FITT-VP, What Matters Most FITT-VP: F requency, I ntensity, T ime, T ype, V olume, P rogression. Dr. Awruch's version answers a narrower question for each category — which single variable actually drives the result.

1. Aerobic / Cardio Variable Recommendation Frequency 3–5 days/week Intensity Moderate–hard. Talk test — can talk, not sing. RPE ~12–16 Time Sessions add up to a weekly total Type Any rhythmic aerobic activity — mode matters less than dose . Road biking vs running, either way it's aerobic Volume — MOST IMPORTANT ≥150 min/week moderate OR ≥75 min/week vigorous Progression Increase time first , then intensity ★ Takeaway: if weekly minutes are too low, intensity doesn't matter. Volume is the variable you increase first.

2. Strength / Resistance Variable Recommendation Frequency 2–3×/week per muscle group Intensity Load heavy enough that the final reps are hard, but not so heavy you get injured — ~6–12 reps close to fatigue Time Defined by reps, sets and rest , not minutes Type Any resistance exercise — exercise choice is secondary Volume — PRIMARY DRIVER ~10–20 hard sets per muscle per week Progression Increase load, reps, or sets over time — not too quickly , or you cause injury or wreck adherence ★ Takeaway: if it's not hard near fatigue, it's not strength training.

3. Mobility / Flexibility Variable Recommendation Frequency ≥2–3 days/week (daily is fine) Intensity Mild–moderate discomfort, no pain . You're not trying to rip muscle, you're trying to increase tissue length Time 30–60 sec per stretch, 2–4 reps Type Static, dynamic, PNF — type matters less Volume — KEY VARIABLE Total time spent at end range Progression More end-range time, more range, or more load ★ Takeaway: range changes because you spend time there. If you never go to a certain range naturally, it's going to be hard to get there. 🎙 The example that stuck with him from school: people who sit a lot at work with their knees bent most of the day may develop tighter hamstrings, because they're not extending their knees very often during the day.

4. Balance / Neuromotor Variable Recommendation Frequency 2–3 days/week Intensity Challenging enough to cause errors. If it isn't, it isn't testing the ability to stay upright Time ~20–30 min/session Type Static · dynamic · reactive (a small push they have to recover from) · dual-task · functional Volume Amount of challenging balance exposure Progression Narrow base → unstable → dual task → faster → unpredictable ★ Takeaway: no errors = no balance training. If the patient never has an error, it might not be challenging enough.

5. Power / Speed Variable Recommendation Main driver Intent to move fast Frequency 1–3 days/week Reps 1–5 — fewer, because power costs much more stress per minute Sets 3–6 Rest Plenty Progression Faster intent → more load → more complexity ★ Takeaway: power is speed, not grinding. Fatigue kills power — you don't want to practise power when already fatigued, and it isn't necessarily the safest. 🎙 The car analogy: accelerating as fast as a car can go is more stressful on the car than driving at a moderate speed on a normal street. That's why high-speed work needs more rest. Where FITT-VP actually sits in your decision making You already have the model that decides whether someone needs mobility or strength — that was Module 3 FITT principles don't create the exercise programme . They influence sets, reps and intensity based on patient response Think of FITT-VP as a progression-regression model , not the way you craft the programme itself “How many sets and reps should I do?” — this is a really nice guide for that question, and that question only 🎙 The snowboard metaphor he apologises for and then lands anyway: learning a backflip meant finding deep snow — a low-stakes environment with a lot of repetitions, where you could fail without getting hurt, use the feedback, and dial it in. That's the balance section of this lecture. It's not balance training if you never fail. And it's what you're doing with patients: something a little harder than what they can already do, but still reachable.

TOPIC 4.2 Aquatic Based Exercise Aquatic therapy is the use of water for rehabilitation — exercises performed in water of various depths within immersion pools or tanks, used to deliver established therapeutic interventions: stretching, strengthening, joint mobilization, endurance training, balance and gait. Named techniques: Bad Ragaz Ring Method · Halliwick Method · WATSU · Aquastretch · Ai Chi · task-oriented approach.

1. Why Water Works — the Properties Property What it does Buoyancy The upward force working opposite to gravity Hydrostatic pressure Pressure exerted by the water on immersed objects Viscosity Resistive drag opposite the direction of movement — resistance is proportional to speed Surface tension The surface acts as a membrane under tension — resistance is increased at the surface Hydromechanics Movement through water creating flow — turbulence, laminar flow, drag Thermodynamics Water is an efficient conductor and transfers heat 25× faster than air Density The body's density is slightly less than water's. More muscle, more density; more body fat, less Centre of buoyancy Where buoyant vertical forces predictably act — the vertical standing position at the level of the sternum ★ Viscosity being proportional to speed is the single most useful property for dosing: the patient controls their own resistance by how fast they move. Move faster, work harder — no equipment change needed.

2. Goals and Indications Range of motion · strengthening · weight bearing for functional activities · manual therapy techniques · cardiovascular aerobic endurance · balance and gait retraining · reducing or relieving pain.

3. Precautions and Contraindications PRECAUTIONS CONTRAINDICATIONS — STOP Fear of water Contagious diseases Cardiac dysfunction · unstable angina · cardiac failure Danger of bleeding or hemorrhage Neurological disorders · seizure disorders Water or airborne infections or diseases Respiratory disorders · severe respiratory dysfunction Peripheral vascular disease · kidney disease Small open wounds and lines · G-tubes and suprapubic appliances · colostomy Bladder and bowel disorders Menstruation or vaginal bleeding Some dermatological or skin infections

s.t: TOPIC 4.3 — Applying FITT-VP to Physical Therapy
s.x: TOPIC 4.3 Applying FITT-VP to Physical Therapy Three application lectures — cardiorespiratory, resistance, and balance. All three open with the same public health baseline: at least 150 minutes of moderate OR 75 minutes of vigorous aerobic exercise per week, AND strength training twice per week.

A. Cardiorespiratory 🎙 The question the deck asks about those guidelines: is this enough to improve cardiorespiratory fitness? To improve fitness you need a dose-response stimulus — usually increasing intensity and/or duration — and you individualise to the patient's starting point.

s.t: 1. Measuring Intensity — the Heart Rate Maths
s.x: 1. Measuring Intensity — the Heart Rate Maths Formula Note Theoretical HRmax = 220 − age Underestimates Tanaka: HRmax = 208 − (0.7 × age) Preferred Heart Rate Reserve: HRR = HRmax − HRrest Measure HR immediately on waking for several days to get HRrest THR = HRR × %intensity + HRrest Preferred THR = HRmax × %intensity Less accurate — doesn't account for resting heart rate The worked example — 54 years old, HRrest 50 HRmax = 208 − (0.7 × 54) = 170.2 (Tanaka) vs 220 − 54 = 166 (the underestimate) HRR = 170.2 − 50 = 120.2 For 65–80% intensity: 120.2 × 0.65 + 50 = 128 bpm (lower), 120.2 × 0.80 + 50 = 146 bpm (upper) Target range 128–146 bpm. The %HRmax method gives 111–136 for the same person — a lower range, because it ignores resting heart rate Variable Recommendation Intensity — moderate 40–59% HRR Intensity — vigorous 60–89% HRR Interval training Work/rest cycles allow higher intensity for shorter periods, increasing total time spent at higher intensities Time 30–60 min moderate/day, 20–60 min vigorous/day, or a mix. Each minute of vigorous = 2 minutes of moderate. Several bouts under 10 minutes are fine Type Individualise — goals, equipment access, interests, health conditions. Add weight-bearing for bone health, cross-training for balance Volume Double the recommendations for benefit: >300 min/week moderate or >150 min/week vigorous. Higher energy expenditure is associated with lower cardiovascular disease and mortality Progression Increase one variable at a time . For previously inactive people, 5–10 min/session every 1–2 weeks for the first month. Monitor for adverse effects ★ Take-home from this deck, stated bluntly: the physical activity guidelines might be insufficient. All activity is good activity, including short bouts. Calculate target heart rate using HRR.

B. Resistance 🎙 The most quotable slide in the module: To improve muscular fitness — strength, hypertrophy, power, local muscular endurance — we need to lift heavy things. We MUST load our patients. LOAD THEM. Term Definition Repetition (rep) A single lift or repetition of an exercise Set A group of reps performed for a single exercise without stopping Repetition maximum (RM) The load that can be lifted a set number of times — 1RM is the load where only one lift can be completed; 10RM the load where ten reps but no more can be performed Goal Intensity Reps / set Sets Rest between sets Strength > 85% 1RM < 6 2–6 2–5 min Power — single lift 80–90% 1RM 1–2 3–5 2–5 min Power — multiple lifts 30–80% 1RM 3–5 3–5 2–5 min Hypertrophy 67–85% 1RM 6–12 3–6 30–90 sec Endurance < 67% 1RM > 12 2–3 < 30 sec Variable Recommendation Frequency > 2×/week. Sedentary individuals can benefit from 1×/week at first due to neural adaptation, but you need more than 2 sessions per week for true gains . Highly trained individuals may need more Prescribing intensity % of a tested RM · RPE · or 'feel' — have them pick a weight they can lift for the requested reps with only 1–2 reps left in the tank Type Machines, free weights, suspension devices, strongman activities, body weight. Enjoyable and accessible · sufficient load · opposing muscle groups · large multi-joint exercises · every major muscle group weekly Volume Limited time or untrained: < 4 sets/week per muscle group . Trained: dose-response, 5–10+ sets/week per muscle group — insufficient evidence beyond that, and a law of diminishing returns Progression One variable at a time — frequency OR intensity OR reps OR sets. 1 day/week may be enough for maintenance ★ Take-home: load your patients. Load them. And do not guess — take the time to individualise the parameters based on current levels.

C. Balance The gap this lecture exists to fill Falls are a huge problem — mortality, morbidity, health care costs, quality of life Yet there are no recommendations for balance in the Physical Activity Guidelines PTs know the importance. So the FITT-VP structure has to be adapted rather than looked up What balance training is: induce instability to practise recovery. You make people uncomfortable and push their limits safely , challenging the different systems — visual, vestibular, somatosensory — to promote positive adaptations, and training positive compensations where needed. Variable How it works for balance Frequency Ambiguous by nature — number of sessions per week, or number of losses of balance per day ? Intensity & Time Inter-related with frequency. Multiple repeated stimuli to destabilise Dose-response Overdose → fear. Underdose → no benefit Type Anticipatory · reactive · exercise-based · functional · tai chi — and not just for people with balance impairments Progression Increase challenge without overwhelming or inducing fear — fear of falling increases fall risk Evidence Finding Gerards et al., *Geriatr Gerontol Int* 2017;17:2294–2303 1 session, 40 slips on a treadmill → no effect on falls. 1 session, multiple ground-based slips → reduced falls Sherrington et al., *Br J Sports Med* 2017;51:1749–1757 >3 hours/week reduced falls long-term 🎙 That is a lot of balance training. Which is exactly why the deck's other instruction is to go back to Movement Science — balance systems, and the motor learning principles of massed vs distributed practice, feedback schedules, type of feedback and stage of learning — and apply those inside your FITT-VP parameters.

TOPIC 4.4 Resistance Exercise and Aging Objectives: describe the changes that occur with aging in skeletal muscle, and begin applying that to modify, focus and optimise strengthening programmes for the older adult.

1. Sarcopenia — Review from Physiology PATHOGENESIS ETIOLOGY Decreased myofiber regeneration Metabolism Selective loss of Type II fibers Endocrine Decreased fiber size Nutrition Impaired excitation-contraction Physical activity Inflammatory markers

s.t: 2. What Aging Does to Skeletal Muscle
s.x: 2. What Aging Does to Skeletal Muscle Increased intermuscular adipose tissue. Lower neuromuscular activation — loss of motor neurons, lower maximal firing rates, poor coordination. Properties of single fibers are preserved , despite reductions in whole-muscle cross-sectional area. Selective atrophy of Type II fibers — smaller and fewer in number. *(Reid et al., Eur J Appl Physiol, 2012)* The headline numbers You lose about 1% of muscle mass per year after age 40 — not too bad, right? Muscle strength decreases three times as fast. Loss of muscle *quality*, linked to mitochondrial loss Exercise can slow this — but not reverse it *(Peterson et al., J Aging Research, 2012)* Study Finding Englund et al., *J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci*, 2018 12 weeks of progressive resistance training improves torque capacity and strength in mobility-limited older adults Moore et al., *J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle*, 2018;9(4):747–754 Low-load resistance exercise over just 6 sessions was associated with increased muscle fiber CSA and capillarization in older adults Roberts et al., *Exp Gerontol*, 2018;106:116–124 Sex differences: females show myofiber atrophy , males show myofiber loss

3. NSCA Position Statement Part Content 1 — Programme variables Resistance exercise is safe for older adults when properly designed . Individualise and work towards: Frequency 2–3×/week · Intensity 70–85% 1RM for strength, 40–60% 1RM for power · Time 2–3 sets of 1–2 multi-joint exercises for each major muscle group · Type progressive resistance strengthening plus higher-velocity power exercises 2 — Physiological adaptations Age-related changes can be counteracted . A well-designed programme enhances muscle strength, power and function. Adaptations are neuromuscular, neuroendocrine and hormonal 3 — Functional benefits Improves mobility, function and performance; helps preserve functional independence ; improves resistance to injury and helps prevent catastrophic events such as falls ; improves psychosocial well-being 4 — Frailty, sarcopenia, chronic conditions Programmes can be adapted and must be individualised . Equipment can be adapted to the living environment — assisted living, skilled nursing facilities *(All four parts: Fragala et al., J Strength Cond Res. 2019 Aug;33(8):2019–2052.)* ★ The slide carries an explicit warning worth repeating: these NSCA numbers are DIFFERENT from the ACSM guidelines. Individualise, and progress TOWARD them — do not start there.

Quick-Reference Glossary — Topic 4.4 Term Definition Sarcopenia Age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and function Type II fiber Fast-twitch fiber — selectively lost with aging Intermuscular adipose tissue Fat deposited between muscle fibers and fascicles, increasing with age Muscle quality Force produced per unit of muscle mass — declines faster than mass itself Capillarization Density of capillaries supplying muscle tissue NSCA National Strength and Conditioning Association Frailty A state of decreased physiologic reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors

TOPIC 5.1 Joint Mechanics 🎙 Why this presentation exists, in the deck's own words: having a strong understanding of joint mechanics can almost be like having a crystal ball — you will soon see the power of how you can predict joint motion based on an understanding of the underlying joint mechanics.

s.t: 1. The Two Words Everything Rests On
s.x: 1. The Two Words Everything Rests On OSTEOKINEMATICS ARTHROKINEMATICS Motion of the bones relative to the planes of the body Motion between the articular surfaces of the joint Also called physiological motion or gross skeletal motion Also called accessory motion , joint mobility , or joint play Describes the movement of body segments A small amount of motion Measured in degrees of freedom — the number of motions available at a joint Highly dependent on the shape and type of the joint Degrees of freedom is determined by the number of planes motion is available in, or the number of axes of rotation. It always ranges from 1 to 3 , since we have three planes and three axes.

2. Joint Classifications Joint type Degrees of freedom Shape Body examples Hinge 1 Resembles a door hinge; one plane, one axis Humeroulnar joint at the elbow · interphalangeal joints of fingers and toes Pivot 1 Allows the single motion of rotation, in the transverse plane Humeroradial joint Ellipsoid 2 Almost a ball and socket, but oblong or elliptical — like an egg. Narrower along one axis, so no rotation about the third Radiocarpal joint at the wrist Ball and socket 3 Round; allows a great deal of mobility in three planes about three axes Glenohumeral joint · coxofemoral (hip) joint Plane 1 or 2 — not always consistent, depends on required function and soft tissue constraints Flat surfaces adjacent to each other Carpometacarpal joints (except the thumb) · intercarpal · intertarsal . Also very common in the spine Saddle 2 Shaped like a rider on a saddle — rocks front-to-back and side-to-side. Shape does not allow axial rotation Thumb (first CMC) · sternoclavicular joint Condyloid 2 More complex — has both concavities and convexities Metacarpophalangeal joints · tibiofemoral joint ★ The lecture is blunt about the expectation: you are responsible for recognising which joint classification applies to EVERY joint in the body — so it's a great time to review your anatomy — plus its degrees of freedom, its available osteokinematic motions, and which planes and axes apply to each motion.

3. The Three Arthrokinematic Motions Motion Definition The mental picture Roll Multiple points on one surface contact multiple points on the other. Essentially the osteokinematic motion A tire rolling on a road, or a ball rolling on a table Slide (glide) A single point on one surface contacts multiple points on the other A tire skidding along a road Spin A single point on one surface rotates on a single point of the other A top spinning in place ★ The one sentence that makes the rest of it solvable: if you can determine the direction the segment is moving in, that will ALWAYS correspond to and match the direction of roll.

4. Convex-Concave — the Rule Itself Joint congruency is the reason this matters. Our joints must fit closely together to provide stability while allowing mobility — fitting like a puzzle, with maximised surface and contact area. Roll without slide, or slide without roll, would destroy that. CONCAVE MOVING ON CONVEX CONVEX MOVING ON CONCAVE Roll and slide occur in the SAME direction Roll and slide occur in OPPOSITE directions Worked example: knee flexion, open chain. The concave tibia moves on the convex femur . Osteokinematic motion is posterior → posterior roll AND posterior slide Worked example: the moving segment goes posteriorly, so roll is posterior — and there is a simultaneous anterior slide 🎙 Why both must happen: if roll occurred without slide, the joint would gap and pull apart. If slide occurred without roll, the distal segment would slide past the proximal one. Either way you lose congruency — the motions must occur together to maintain the integrity of the joint.

s.t: 5. Open Chain vs Closed Chain — the Reversal
s.x: 5. Open Chain vs Closed Chain — the Reversal We assess primarily in open chain , and passively — muscle action would otherwise influence the arthrokinematic motion. In open chain the distal segment is free and moving on the proximal segment. The reversal, at the tibiofemoral joint Open chain: concave tibia moving on convex femur → roll and slide in the same direction Closed chain: convex femur moving on concave tibia → roll and slide in opposite directions The structures haven't changed. What's moving relative to the other has changed. 🎙 Functionally you might detect mobility limitations in closed chain, and these can be due to arthrokinematic limitations or muscle activation patterns, or both. You will eventually need to look at this from both views. ★ The assigned Neumann opinion article is required reading specifically because Dr. Neumann addresses why it is still worth teaching and learning the convex-concave patterns to guide treatment — even though they are not perfect and have real limitations.

Quick-Reference Glossary — Topic 5.1 Term Definition Osteokinematics Motion of bones relative to the body's planes; physiological or gross skeletal motion Arthrokinematics Motion between articular surfaces; accessory motion, joint play Degrees of freedom Number of independent motions available at a joint; 1 to 3 Roll Multiple points on multiple points; matches the direction of the osteokinematic motion Slide (glide) One point on the moving surface travelling across multiple points of the stable one Spin Rotation of one point on a single point of the opposing surface Joint congruency How closely the articular surfaces fit, maximising contact area for stability Concave-convex rule Concave on convex: roll and slide the same direction Convex-concave rule Convex on concave: roll and slide opposite directions Open chain Distal segment free, moving on a fixed proximal segment Closed chain Distal segment fixed; the proximal segment moves on it, reversing the rule Open-packed position The loosest, least congruent joint position Close-packed position The position of maximum congruency and capsular tautness

s.t: TOPIC 5.2 — Mechanics of the Peripheral Joints
s.x: TOPIC 5.2 Mechanics of the Peripheral Joints Five regional lectures from Dr. Andreyo . The study guide narrows what you're accountable for: primary knee and shoulder, ankle also important, spine secondary. The regional detail below is ordered accordingly.

Tibiofemoral Joint Property Detail Classification Hinge joint — distal femur moving on the proximal tibia Degrees of freedom 2 — flexion/extension, and internal/external rotation Open-packed position 25° shy of full extension — the loosest position Close-packed position Full extension and external rotation — most taut on the capsule Flexion/extension Sagittal plane. The axis migrates with the degree of flexion, because the condyle isn't perfectly spherical — so torque differs through range Expected ROM Full extension = 0° , or up to about 5° of hyperextension . Flexion to about 140° Rotation Transverse plane , and unlike flexion/extension this is a fixed axis . Internal rotation ~ 25° , external up to ~ 45° . More flexion or extension puts tension on the capsule and restricts rotation Chain Relationship Extension Flexion Open Concave tibia on convex femur — same direction Anterior roll + anterior slide Posterior roll + posterior slide Closed Convex femur on concave tibia — opposite directions Posterior slide Anterior slide

The Screw-Home Mechanism The knee very rarely moves purely in the sagittal plane. To reach full extension it must use the screw-home mechanism: through the last ~30° of extension , the articular surfaces require a small amount of rotation because they are not equal surfaces. OPEN CHAIN CLOSED CHAIN As the leg goes into extension, the tibia must externally rotate The inverse — the femur must internally rotate 🎙 Both transcripts render this as “screw hole mechanism.” That is a transcription artifact — the term is screw-home. These notes use the correct term.

Patellofemoral Joint A plane joint — analogous to a book moving on a table, though the condyles make it more of a divot. The patella slides in a groove. Knee motion Patella moves So to improve it… Flexion Pulled inferiorly Extension Pulled superiorly Mobilize the patella superiorly — that's the direction it wants to move Because it's a plane joint it has more motions than the obvious one: superior-inferior in the sagittal plane, plus tilt side to side, medial-lateral shift , and a very small amount of rotation in the groove. 🎙 The patella is a sesamoid bone sitting within tissue, so it moves with that tissue — which is why so many external forces are pulling on it to say where it should and shouldn't go. Tight laterally-directed structures such as the iliotibial band can pull it laterally and alter how well it sits centred in the groove. Compressive forces: the more flexion you go into, the more the patella is pulled in toward the knee joint, creating tension across the quadriceps and patellar tendons and more compressive force at the joint .

B. The Shoulder Complex Four joints in one region: glenohumeral, acromioclavicular, sternoclavicular, scapulothoracic. Very rarely does a shoulder movement involve only one of them. Property Glenohumeral joint Classification Ball and socket , 3 degrees of freedom — though the deck notes it looks less like a ball in a socket and more like a golf ball sitting on a tee Congruency Very little bony congruency — a small glenoid relative to a large humeral head. Great mobility, and therefore more instability Stabilisers Glenoid labrum deepens the surface with softer tissue. Robust ligaments anteriorly , substantial muscular structures posteriorly Open-packed position Slight abduction and horizontal adduction — i.e. the scapular plane Close-packed position Full abduction and external rotation Osteokinematics Flexion/extension · abduction/adduction · internal/external rotation — usually in combination Arthrokinematics Convex humeral head on concave glenoid → roll and slide in OPPOSITE directions. Abduction gives a superior roll and an inferior glide ★ The inferior glide with abduction is the one to lock in — it's why glenohumeral inferior and posterior glides are on the practical's core skills checklist.

C. The Ankle Property Talocrural joint Articulation Distal tibia and fibula on the talus Degrees of freedom Predominantly 1 — dorsiflexion / plantarflexion Open-packed position Slight plantarflexion Close-packed position Maximal dorsiflexion Open chain Convex talar head on concave tibia/fibula → opposite directions. Dorsiflexion = anterior roll + posterior glide Closed chain Concave tibia on convex talus → same direction. Dorsiflexion = anterior roll + anterior slide ★ This is exactly why the practical lists a talocrural POSTERIOR glide (including the mobilization-with-movement concept) as the skill for limited dorsiflexion — and it's the correction to the Module 1 Canvas page, which mistakenly names the calcaneus. Subtalar joint — talus on calcaneus. The lecture flags a genuine complication: the posterior facet is a concave talus on a convex calcaneus , while the anterior and middle facets are the opposite . Do they cancel out? Do you address the posterior facet because it's larger? For simplicity the course treats it as a plane joint , and unpacks it further in joint mobilization.

D. The Elbow Articulation Relationship Flexion Humeroulnar Concave ulna on convex humerus — same direction Roll and glide both anterior . Reverse for extension Humeroradial Concave radius on convex humerus — same direction Roll and slide both anterior Proximal radioulnar Convex radius on concave — opposite directions Roll anterior → glide posterior 🎙 Upper extremity mechanics are taught in open chain because that's how we use the arm functionally — not to discredit closed-chain upper extremity movement, which comes back in upper extremity MSK.

E. Wrist and Hand Property Detail Radiocarpal classification Ellipsoid — two main directions of movement Motions Flexion/extension and ulnar/radial deviation Resting position Neutral with slight ulnar deviation — put your hand flat on a desk and that's it Arthrokinematics Proximal row is a convexity moving on the concavity of the radius → roll and slide in opposite directions Axis of rotation The capitate Midcarpal joint Between the proximal and distal rows — follows the same pattern as the radiocarpal joint Ulnar variance Most of the articulation is on the radius , not the ulna — relevant to load distribution

F. Choosing Manual Therapy & Exercise Dr. Awruch's decision pathway, tying Modules 3–5 together. Rule 1: start with what you see. Osteokinematics is what looks limited, painful or asymmetric — observe and measure the movement first. Step The question The answer Entry — MSK screen Start with the limited or painful motion (e.g. knee flexion). Is it a ROM problem, a pain problem, or both? ROM problem = “can't get there” (stiffness/limitation). Pain problem = “won't go there” (sensitivity/irritability). Measure with goniometry and symptom report, decide which limiter is primary Step 2 — the bucket If it's a ROM issue, what's limiting it? Tissue = muscle length / soft tissue → stretching, active mobility, STM. Joint = painful or hypomobile → manual therapy, and then: which bone is moving? Tip: use a gentle mob as a *test* — does it change symptoms or ROM? Step 3 — access method Manual therapy and exercise are not a hierarchy — different methods, same target Assisted access (manual): mobilization (usually a glide) · MWM · traction/distraction · manipulation (future class). Owned access (exercise): active mobility in the same direction · isometrics/gentle/partial range if sensitive · progress with FITT Steps 4–6 Access → re-test → ownership Access: find the motion with the least symptoms. Re-test: repeat the same movement immediately — did ROM improve, did pain drop? Ownership: give a patient-performed drill for the same target motion ROM Pain Do this ↓ Limited ↑ High Assisted access + a supported owned version ↓ Limited ↓ Low Mobility + build capacity (progress) Full ↑ High Pain modulation + graded exposure Full ↓ Low Strength / load / skill — skip mechanics entirely ★ Avoid random-exercise thinking. Be target-motion specific, confirm with an immediate re-test, then build capacity. Manual is assisted access; exercise is independent ownership. Same goal, different delivery.

s.t: 3. Why Open vs Closed Chain Matters (Three Reasons)
s.x: 3. Why Open vs Closed Chain Matters (Three Reasons) To name the position for communication — open chain vs closed chain. To answer roll vs glide questions — which bone is moving. To pick a glide direction that biases the motion you want to improve — focus on shoulder, knee, ankle. MOBILIZATION — THE SIMPLE DEFINITION THE TWO MAIN WAYS The therapist uses their hands to help a stiff or painful joint move better 1. PROM with overpressure — move the limb through the motion, often near end range 2. A small joint-specific push or pull (a glide) to bias the direction you want — directional thinking only , you don't need the full slide-glide chart 🎙 Why we learned glides: glides help you think about direction now. The next module connects that direction thinking to actual manual techniques.

4. The Practical Exam Guide Read this first, to reduce studying stress Skills and exam questions come ONLY from class resources — Canvas modules, lab videos, handouts, slides, in-class labs If you hear an exercise or technique mentioned from outside the course, treat it as an example only If a skill is not on the Core Skills Checklist, it will not be expected on the practical What is graded Detail Clinical reasoning Choose the right intervention bucket based on the main limiter — ROM deficit vs strength deficit vs high pain Safe setup + execution Positioning, therapist mechanics, cues, patient safety Progression/regression Make a logical change based on patient response Bucket Core skills to demonstrate AND explain Pain modulation / fear Shoulder pendulums · gentle shoulder or knee AROM · grade I mobilization Mobility — tissue extensibility PROM assessment (shoulder or knee) · hamstring stretch (self or manual) · Ely's / rectus femoris stretch (self or manual) Mobility — joint Glenohumeral posterior OR inferior glide · talocrural posterior glide (including the MWM concept) · lumbar PA glides · knee flexion OR extension mobilization . *No patient self/home versions of joint mobilizations are required* Strength / stability Regular AROM of the target joint is a valid strengthening answer. Progression: AAROM → AROM → RROM . Lower extremity: lunge sequence, lateral band walks, side-lying hip abduction. Upper extremity: rotator cuff ER, mid-trap T , lower-trap Y SCOPE NOT ON THE PRACTICAL Most focus is on shoulder and knee ; ankle may appear depending on the case Thoracic manual therapy — safety and exposure only Skills from other modules may be asked as “please perform this skill” — not as a case Level 3 performance/testing — hop testing, cone drills, plyometrics: recognise appropriate use, not a performance expectation Any skill not on the Core Skills Checklist ★ Two reassurances stated outright in the guide. You are assessed on decision-making and safety, not perfect technique for every variation. And you will not be double- or triple-dinged: choosing the wrong bucket costs points there, but you don't keep losing points for being on the wrong road. Step What happens Prep Sign in, receive your case, use prep time to identify the main limiter + bucket Day 1 Identify impairment bucket and task; pick 3 interventions — the exact exercise can vary, but the bucket selection should be correct Day 2 Proctor prompts a status change, better or worse. Regress or progress logically Day 3 Second status change. Same reasoning process The simple case script Bucket: ____ because ____ (main limiter) Direction / target: ____ (what needs to change) Intervention: ____ (choose from core skills) Re-test: ____ (the same metric) If better: progress ____ / If worse: regress ____ — with a clear why
